nodes.label: Ter-Petrosyan
nodes.full: Levon Ter-Petrosyan, a philologist and a leader of the Karabakh Committee and of the Armenian National Movement, was elected the first president of independent Armenia on 16 October 1991 and re-elected in a disputed vote on 22 September 1996. He led the country through the war, the blockade and the energy crisis, and resigned on 3 February 1998 after his defence, interior and security ministers opposed his support for a phased settlement of the Karabakh question proposed by the OSCE.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (1991, 1996); Ter-Petrosyan, statement of 3 February 1998; Thomas de Waal, Black Garden (2003).

nodes.label: Kocharyan
nodes.full: Robert Kocharyan, who had led the self-declared Republic of Nagorno-Karabakh as its president from 1994 and had been prime minister of Armenia since 1997, was elected president in the second round of March 1998 and re-elected in 2003, in a vote the opposition and some observers criticised. His decade saw the assassinations of 1999, the constitutional amendments of 2005, double-digit economic growth in the mid-2000s and the rise of the closely allied business and political circle later called the oligarchs. After the 2018 revolution he was charged in connection with the events of 1 March 2008, a case that was reshaped and then largely dropped after a Constitutional Court ruling in 2021.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (1998, 2003); OSCE/ODIHR election reports; de Waal 2003; reports on the case of 1 March 2008 (2018–2021).

nodes.label: Serzh Sargsyan
nodes.full: Serzh Sargsyan, a Karabakh veteran who had been defence and interior minister, was elected president on 19 February 2008 in an election followed by the violence of 1 March, and re-elected in 2013. He steered the constitutional change of 2015 from a presidential to a parliamentary system and after his second term moved to the post of prime minister on 17 April 2018; he resigned on 23 April, after weeks of mass street protests, saying that Nikol Pashinyan had been right and he had been wrong.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2008, 2013); Sargsyan's resignation statement (23 April 2018); OSCE/ODIHR reports.

nodes.label: Sarkissian
nodes.full: Armen Sarkissian, a physicist, former prime minister and ambassador to Britain, was elected by parliament in March 2018 as the last president under the old rules and the first in the new parliamentary republic, which made the office largely ceremonial. In January 2022 he resigned, saying that he lacked the means to influence events in a time of crisis, and was succeeded by Vahagn Khachaturyan.
nodes.src: National Assembly records (2 March 2018); Sarkissian's resignation letter (January 2022).

nodes.label: Khachaturyan
nodes.full: Vahagn Khachaturyan, a former ambassador nominated by the ruling Civil Contract party, was elected by parliament on 3 March 2022 and took office on 13 March for a seven-year term. As of 2026 he is head of state in a system where the president represents the country and has few executive powers, which are held by the prime minister.
nodes.src: National Assembly records (3 March 2022); Constitution of Armenia (2015), articles 123–137.

nodes.label: Governments of the first republic
nodes.full: Prime ministers of the first years included Hrant Bagratyan (1993–1996), an economist who introduced the dram on 22 November 1993 and led the macro-stabilisation and the privatisation, Armen Sarkissian (1996–1997) and Robert Kocharyan from 1997. They governed under the blockade and the energy shortage, with a presidential office whose powers were enlarged by the constitution of 1995.
nodes.src: Government records; Edmund Herzig, The New Caucasus (1999); Hrant Bagratyan, memoirs and interviews.

nodes.label: Governments of the Republican era
nodes.full: After Vazgen Sargsyan, killed in the parliament on 27 October 1999, the prime ministers were Andranik Margaryan (2000–2007, who died in office), Serzh Sargsyan (2007–2008), Tigran Sargsyan (2008–2014), Hovik Abrahamyan (2014–2016) and Karen Karapetyan (2016–2018). Republican Party rule, which relied on a coalition with Prosperous Armenia and the Dashnaktsutyun at various times, was accused by opponents of corruption and by supporters credited with growth and stability.
nodes.src: Government and National Assembly records; Transparency International and OSCE reports; Laurence Broers, Armenia and Azerbaijan: Anatomy of a Rivalry (2019).

nodes.label: Pashinyan
nodes.full: Nikol Pashinyan, a journalist and opposition deputy who led the protests of April 2018, was elected prime minister by parliament on 8 May 2018. His My Step alliance took about 70 per cent of the vote in the snap election of 9 December 2018, his Civil Contract about 54 per cent in the snap election of 20 June 2021 after the war, and, according to the results of 7 June 2026, about 50 per cent and a parliamentary majority below two thirds, a result the opposition has contested. As of 2026 he is prime minister and the central figure of the peace process.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2018, 2021, 2026); OSCE/ODIHR statements.

nodes.label: First Karabakh war
nodes.full: After the dissolution of the Soviet Union the conflict that began in 1988 became a full war: the Karabakh Armenians declared a republic after a referendum of 10 December 1991 that the Azerbaijani population boycotted, and Armenian forces and Karabakh's Defence Army, supported by volunteers and by Armenia, took Shusha on 8–9 May 1992, opened the Lachin corridor, and in 1993 occupied Kelbajar and districts beyond Karabakh's borders. The UN Security Council resolutions 822, 853, 874 and 884 of 1993 demanded withdrawal; the Bishkek Protocol and ceasefire of 12 May 1994 followed. The Armenian side describes the war as self-determination and defence of a population threatened with exile, the Azerbaijani side as an aggression and occupation of about a fifth of its territory; estimates of the dead range from about 20,000 to 30,000, and hundreds of thousands were displaced on both sides.
nodes.src: UN Security Council resolutions 822, 853, 874, 884 (1993); Bishkek Protocol (1994); de Waal 2003; Human Rights Watch, Azerbaijan: Seven Years of Conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh (1994).

nodes.label: Maragha
nodes.full: On 10 April 1992 Azerbaijani units took the Armenian village of Maragha in northern Karabakh; Armenian and some independent accounts speak of several dozen villagers killed or taken hostage, with figures of about 40–50 given, while the Azerbaijani side presented the events as part of the military action and has disputed the characterisation. The killing of Azerbaijani civilians at Khojaly in February 1992 is treated in the Azerbaijan folio; the two cases are remembered on each side as a separate crime and are the subject of continuing disagreement about numbers and responsibility.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch reports (1992–1994); Memorial reports; de Waal 2003.

nodes.label: Shooting in the parliament
nodes.full: On 27 October 1999 five gunmen led by the former journalist Nairi Hunanyan entered the National Assembly during a session and killed Prime Minister Vazgen Sargsyan, Speaker Karen Demirchyan, two deputy speakers and four other officials, eight people in all; they surrendered after a night of negotiations with President Kocharyan. They were sentenced to life imprisonment in 2003. The reasons and the question of who stood behind the gunmen remain contested, and the trial did not answer them to the satisfaction of the victims' families.
nodes.src: Court verdict (2003); Human Rights Watch and Council of Europe reports; Armenian press accounts.

nodes.label: 1 March 2008
nodes.full: After the election of 19 February 2008 the former president Levon Ter-Petrosyan, who was the main opposition candidate, and his supporters held a camp in the centre of Yerevan, and when police and troops dispersed it on the morning of 1 March, fighting spread and ten people (eight protesters and two members of the security forces) were killed; Kocharyan declared a state of emergency for twenty days. An inquiry of the Council of Europe in 2009 and further court cases after 2018 treated the question of responsibility, which is not settled.
nodes.src: Council of Europe PACE Resolution 1643 (2009); OSCE/ODIHR report (2008); Human Rights Watch, Democracy on Rocky Ground (2009).

nodes.label: Electric Yerevan and Sasna Tsrer
nodes.full: In June 2015 tens of thousands of young people held a sit-in in Baghramyan Avenue against an increase in electricity prices in a market owned by a Russian company, and the movement was dispersed by water cannon on 23 June and ended with the government's decision to cover the rise from the budget. On 17 July 2016 the Sasna Tsrer group, armed veterans and opposition activists, took over a police station in Erebuni demanding the release of the opposition leader Jirair Sefilian and the resignation of Serzh Sargsyan; three policemen were killed, and the group surrendered on 31 July, with large crowds in support.
nodes.src: Armenian and international press (2015–2016); OSCE and Human Rights Watch statements; court records of the Sasna Tsrer trial.

nodes.label: Velvet Revolution
nodes.full: When Serzh Sargsyan, after two terms as president, was made prime minister under the new constitution, the opposition deputy Nikol Pashinyan began a march from Gyumri to Yerevan on 31 March 2018 under the slogan My Step; after mass rallies, civil disobedience and the joining of the protests by some soldiers and by crowds in every part of the country, Sargsyan resigned on 23 April and parliament elected Pashinyan prime minister on 8 May. It was an almost entirely non-violent transfer of power and is usually called the Velvet Revolution.
nodes.src: Press and wire reports (April–May 2018); National Assembly records (8 May 2018); Broers 2019.

nodes.label: Four-day war
nodes.full: In the heaviest fighting since 1994 Azerbaijani forces attacked along the line of contact on 2 April 2016 and took heights near Talish and in the south at Lalatapa before a ceasefire mediated by Russia on 5 April; Armenia reported 92 soldiers killed and Azerbaijan 31, with independent estimates higher and civilian victims on both sides. The two states and the Minsk Group co-chairs described the fighting in contrasting ways, Armenia as a large-scale attack and Azerbaijan as a response to shelling.
nodes.src: Ministries of defence of Armenia and Azerbaijan (April 2016); OSCE Minsk Group co-chairs' statements; Broers 2019.

nodes.label: Second Karabakh war
nodes.full: The war began on 27 September 2020, with Azerbaijan and Armenia each blaming the other for the first shots; Azerbaijani forces, with Turkish and Israeli drones and with Turkish political support, took the districts of Jebrail, Fuzuli, Zangilan and Gubadli and the town of Hadrut and on 8 November Shusha. Through a statement signed on 9–10 November by Aliyev, Pashinyan and Putin, Armenia ceded Agdam, Kelbajar and the Lachin district, Russian peacekeepers were deployed in what remained of Karabakh, and a transport link through Armenia's Syunik was foreseen. The official counts of the military dead were 3,825 on the Armenian and 2,783 on the Azerbaijani side, with several hundred civilians killed on both sides and reports of war crimes and mistreatment of prisoners that each side has denied or blamed on the other.
nodes.src: Trilateral statement (10 November 2020); defence ministries of Armenia and Azerbaijan; Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reports (2020–2021); Broers 2021.

nodes.label: Attacks of September 2022
nodes.full: On 12–14 September 2022 Azerbaijan shelled and attacked Armenian territory along the border at Jermuk, Goris, Vardenis and Sotk and took positions inside Armenia, in the largest attack on the country's internationally recognised territory since independence; the toll was reported by Armenia as about 135–200 soldiers killed or missing and about 80 for Azerbaijan, with several thousand civilians displaced. Azerbaijan said it was responding to Armenian provocations and the alleged mining of roads; a ceasefire was reached on 13 September after Russian, American and European mediation.
nodes.src: Ministries of defence of Armenia and Azerbaijan; statements of Pashinyan (16 September 2022); EU Mission in Armenia (2023–) reports.

nodes.label: Lachin corridor blockade
nodes.full: From 12 December 2022 a group presenting itself as Azerbaijani environmental activists blocked the road linking Karabakh with Armenia, and from 23 April 2023 Azerbaijan set up a checkpoint at the corridor's entrance; the 120,000 inhabitants were cut off from supplies of food, fuel and medicine for nine months. Armenia and the Karabakh authorities called it a blockade and a deliberate starvation, the International Court of Justice ordered Azerbaijan on 22 February 2023 to ensure unimpeded movement along the corridor, and Azerbaijan denied that it was a blockade and said the road was open to the Red Cross and the Russian peacekeepers and that supplies could come by the Agdam road.
nodes.src: ICJ order of 22 February 2023; UN and ICRC statements; statements of the governments of Armenia and Azerbaijan.

nodes.label: Offensive and exodus
nodes.full: On 19 September 2023 Azerbaijan launched what it called an anti-terror operation in Karabakh, and on 20 September the Karabakh authorities agreed to surrender their arms and negotiate; in the following days some 100,000 of the roughly 120,000 Armenians left for Armenia, and an explosion at a fuel depot near Stepanakert on 25 September killed, by the Karabakh authorities' count, some 170 people as crowds queued for fuel. Armenia, the Karabakh authorities and many observers called it an ethnic cleansing; Azerbaijan denied it and said the residents had been invited to stay as citizens and had left on their own. The republic was dissolved by its own decree effective 1 January 2024 and the Russian peacekeepers left in June 2024.
nodes.src: Statements of the Karabakh authorities (28 September 2023); UN visiting mission report (October 2023); UNHCR figures; Azerbaijan presidential administration statements.

nodes.label: Independence referendum
nodes.full: On 23 August 1990 the Supreme Council adopted the Declaration of Independence, which also stated the Unification Act of 1989 of Armenia with Nagorno-Karabakh, and after the failed coup in Moscow the referendum of 21 September 1991 produced a vote of about 99 per cent for independence at a turnout of about 95 per cent; the Supreme Council declared independence on 23 September. The declaration of 1990 is cited in the preamble of the constitution and is the point in the later peace discussions where Azerbaijan demands a change.
nodes.src: Declaration of Independence (23 August 1990); referendum results (21 September 1991); Constitution of Armenia (1995, 2015), preamble.

nodes.label: Constitutions of 1995 to 2015
nodes.full: The constitution of 5 July 1995, adopted by referendum, gave the president wide powers; the amendments of 27 November 2005, partly shaped by the Council of Europe, reduced some of them; the referendum of 6 December 2015 turned the republic into a parliamentary one from 2018, with a ceremonial president and a prime minister, and was approved with about 66 per cent at a turnout of about 50 per cent, with opponents saying that it was a means for Serzh Sargsyan to stay in power.
nodes.src: Constitutions of Armenia (1995, 2015); referendum records (2005, 2015); Venice Commission opinions.

nodes.label: Disputed elections
nodes.full: The presidential elections of 1996, 2003, 2008 and 2013 and the parliamentary elections of 1995, 1999 and 2007 were criticised by international observers for violations, and the result of 1996 was followed by protests, a state of emergency and tanks in Yerevan; the elections of December 2018 and June 2021, held after the revolution and the war, were judged by the OSCE as competitive and generally well run, though in 2021 with polarised rhetoric and some misuse of administrative resources, and the opposition did not accept the results.
nodes.src: OSCE/ODIHR election observation mission reports (1996–2021).

nodes.label: Ban of the Dashnaktsutyun
nodes.full: In December 1994 President Ter-Petrosyan suspended the Armenian Revolutionary Federation (Dashnaktsutyun), the oldest of the parties and the main diaspora party, for six months, and closed its newspaper Yerkir, after accusing it of running a secret group named Dro that engaged in drug trade and political killings; the party denied it and the ban, which was extended, was lifted by President Kocharyan in 1998. It is cited as one of the early cases of the use of administrative measures in political competition.
nodes.src: Presidential decree (28 December 1994); Helsinki Watch and US State Department reports (1995–1997); Herzig 1999.

nodes.label: Council of Europe
nodes.full: Armenia and Azerbaijan were admitted to the Council of Europe on 25 January 2001, with commitments on the rights of prisoners, the courts and, by Armenia, the abolition of capital punishment; executions were halted from 1991 under a moratorium, the penalty was removed from the criminal code in 2003, and Armenia later ratified the relevant protocols of the European Convention.
nodes.src: Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly Opinion 221 (2000); Criminal Code of Armenia (2003).

nodes.label: Crisis after the war
nodes.full: After the statement of 9–10 November 2020 crowds stormed the government building and the parliament and the speaker was attacked; the opposition demanded Pashinyan's resignation, and on 25 February 2021, when he moved to dismiss the chief of the general staff, the army's high command issued a statement asking him to leave, which he called an attempted coup. The crisis was resolved by the snap elections of 20 June 2021, which Civil Contract won.
nodes.src: Press and wire reports (November 2020–June 2021); OSCE/ODIHR report (2021).

nodes.label: Peace treaty and the preamble
nodes.full: The text of a treaty on peace and interstate relations, initialled by the foreign ministers in Washington on 8 August 2025 and not signed or ratified as of October 2026, is accompanied by the demand of Azerbaijan, which says that it will sign the treaty only after Armenia removes from its constitution the reference to the Declaration of Independence of 1990 and with it, as Baku reads it, a territorial claim. Pashinyan proposes a new constitution and a referendum, which are planned for 2027; the opposition and parts of the church say this would be a concession under pressure that threatens the national identity, and the government presents a new constitution as a sovereign choice to build the state of what it calls the Real Armenia.
nodes.src: Joint declaration of Washington (8 August 2025); statements of Pashinyan and Aliyev (2025–2026); Armenian press reports.

nodes.label: 1700th anniversary
nodes.full: The Armenian Apostolic Church, led since 1999 by Catholicos Karekin II after Karekin I, celebrated in 2001 the 1700th anniversary of the conversion of Armenia under Tiridates and Gregory the Illuminator, with the consecration of the new Cathedral of St Gregory the Illuminator in Yerevan and a visit of Pope John Paul II on 25–27 September, the first papal visit to the country. The church holds a special constitutional status as the national church, and its attendance and the influence of its leaders are often cited in the public life of the state.
nodes.src: Holy See and Etchmiadzin statements (2001); Constitution of Armenia (2015), chapter 1.

nodes.label: Canonisation of the martyrs
nodes.full: On 23 April 2015, the eve of the centenary of the beginning of the mass killings of 1915, the Armenian Church canonised the victims of the genocide, an act of unprecedented scale, in a ceremony at Etchmiadzin attended by Catholicos Karekin II and Catholicos Aram I of Cilicia; days earlier, on 12 April, Pope Francis had called the killings the first genocide of the twentieth century, which Turkey rejected.
nodes.src: Etchmiadzin statement (2015); Holy See, homily of 12 April 2015.

nodes.label: Church and government
nodes.full: From 2025 Prime Minister Pashinyan repeatedly called on Catholicos Karekin II to resign and accused some of the clergy of a plot; Archbishop Bagrat Galstanyan, who had led a movement against the border changes, and Archbishop Mikael Ajapahyan were arrested in June 2025, and Ajapahyan was convicted of calling for the overthrow of the government and sentenced to two years. Another archbishop was detained in December 2025, and on 14 February 2026 the Catholicos himself was indicted on a charge related to his decision to defrock a bishop. The church and the opposition say it is a campaign against the church and a breach of the separation of church and state; the government says the prosecutions concern crimes unrelated to faith and a political attempt, supported from Moscow, to overthrow it. As of 2026 the cases are not resolved.
nodes.src: Reuters, AsiaNews and Armenian press reports (June 2025–February 2026); statements of the Mother See and of the government.

nodes.label: Cascade and Cafesjian Center
nodes.full: The Cafesjian Center for the Arts, opened in November 2009 inside the giant stairway known as the Cascade, which had been designed by Jim Torosyan and others from the 1970s and left unfinished after 1991, was the most visible cultural project funded by the diaspora, the philanthropist Gerard Cafesjian, and gave Yerevan a collection of contemporary art and a new place for the city's life; its ownership later became the subject of a legal dispute between the foundation and the state.
nodes.src: Cafesjian Center for the Arts documents; Armenian press reports.

nodes.label: Aznavour and Tankian
nodes.full: Charles Aznavour, born in Paris to Armenian parents and the best known singer of the diaspora, was named a Hero of Armenia in 2004, was the country's ambassador to Switzerland and delegate to the UN in Geneva from 2009 and died in October 2018; Serj Tankian of System of a Down brought the genocide's memory to a rock audience, and the group's concert in Yerevan on 23 April 2015 was one of the events of the centenary.
nodes.src: Presidential decree (2004); Armenian and international press reports.

nodes.label: Eurovision
nodes.full: Armenia first entered the Eurovision Song Contest in 2006 and reached the top five several times, with Sirusho's fourth place in 2008; it withdrew from the contest of 2012, held in Baku, citing security, and in 2015 its entry by the group Genealogy, whose members were from five continents and meant to represent the diaspora of the genocide's descendants, was a part of the centenary.
nodes.src: European Broadcasting Union contest records (2006–2015).

nodes.label: Chess
nodes.full: The Armenian team won the Chess Olympiad in Turin (2006), Dresden (2008) and Istanbul (2012), and Levon Aronian was for years among the world's top players; in 2011 Armenia was the first country to make chess a compulsory subject in the primary schools, building on the memory of Tigran Petrosian, the world champion from 1963 to 1969.
nodes.src: FIDE Olympiad records; Ministry of Education decree (2011).

nodes.label: Genocide recognition
nodes.full: The recognition of the killings of 1915 as genocide became the main theme of Armenia's foreign policy and the diaspora's work: France recognised it in law in 2001, the Bundestag in 2016, both houses of the US Congress in October and December 2019 and President Biden formally on 24 April 2021, while Turkey rejects the term and describes the events as a wartime tragedy of all peoples, calling for a joint commission of historians. The centenary of 2015 brought leaders including Putin and Hollande to Yerevan.
nodes.src: Parliamentary and congressional resolutions (2001–2019); White House statement (24 April 2021); Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements.

nodes.label: Real Armenia
nodes.full: Since 2023 Pashinyan has argued that the state should be built on what he calls the real Armenia, the country within its internationally recognised borders, and not on the historical Armenia of memory and territorial aspiration, and that peace requires giving up the latter in the constitution; critics, among them the church and the diaspora parties, call it an abandonment of the national project and of Karabakh, and supporters call it a necessary realism after the wars. The debate is still open.
nodes.src: Speeches and interviews of Pashinyan (2023–2026); Armenian press and commentary.

nodes.label: Complementarity
nodes.full: Kocharyan's foreign minister Vartan Oskanian developed in the late 1990s the policy of complementarity, which aimed to hold the security alliance with Russia, relations with the United States and Europe, and ties with Iran and Georgia at once; its test came in September 2013, when Serzh Sargsyan announced after a meeting with Putin that Armenia would join the Eurasian customs union instead of signing an association agreement with the European Union, and again after 2020 and 2022, when the loss of confidence in the Russian guarantee pushed Pashinyan to a Western turn.
nodes.src: Speeches of Oskanian; Joint statement Sargsyan–Putin (3 September 2013); Broers 2019.

nodes.label: Dark and cold years
nodes.full: With the earthquake's damage, the loss of the Soviet market and the blockade by Azerbaijan and Turkey, which had closed the borders in 1993, the economy contracted by more than half between 1990 and 1993; in the winters of 1992–1995 the households had electricity for a few hours a day, trees in Yerevan were cut for fuel, and the period is remembered in Armenia as the dark and cold years until the Metsamor plant was restarted in November 1995.
nodes.src: World Bank and IMF country reports (1993–1997); Herzig 1999.

nodes.label: Privatisation
nodes.full: Collective farms were divided among rural households in the land reform of 1991–1993, which made Armenia a country of small farms, and the voucher privatisation of state enterprises in 1994–1998 was followed by sales to insiders and to Russian companies; in 2002 several enterprises were transferred to Russia in settlement of a debt of about 98 million dollars. The imports of fuel, sugar, flour and other goods came to be controlled by a few well-connected businessmen, a feature that the 2018 revolution targeted.
nodes.src: World Bank reports; Armenian government and parliament records; Transparency International reports.

nodes.label: Mining and Amulsar
nodes.full: Copper, molybdenum and gold have been the main exports of Armenia, and the opening of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine in Lori, which required the cutting of forest, and of the Amulsar gold mine near Jermuk, which was blocked by local protesters from 2018 for fear for the waters of the Jermuk spa and the rivers of the basin, became the main environmental conflicts of the republic. The mining company argued that the project was safe and the blockade illegal, and after 2018 the government commissioned an independent expert review; the company Lydian entered insolvency proceedings in 2019.
nodes.src: Armenian government and company reports; Lydian International statements; Armenian and international press.

nodes.label: IT economy and the 2022 boom
nodes.full: From the early 2000s the Soviet legacy of computing and mathematics and a diaspora of engineers built an information-technology sector that by the 2020s was among the fastest-growing in the economy, with several per cent of gross domestic product; the arrival in 2022 of tens of thousands of Russians and of Russian companies after the invasion of Ukraine, together with re-exports, raised official growth to about 12 per cent in 2022, and the effects on prices and rents were the subject of debate.
nodes.src: Armenian Statistical Committee; IMF and World Bank reports (2022–2023).

nodes.label: Metsamor
nodes.full: The nuclear plant at Metsamor, built in 1976–1980 and shut down after the earthquake of 1988, was restarted with one reactor on 5 November 1995 to end the energy crisis; it supplies roughly a third of the country's electricity, its Soviet-type reactor is criticised by the European Union and by neighbouring Turkey for safety reasons, and the government has extended the life of the unit and discussed a replacement.
nodes.src: Armenian Nuclear Regulatory Authority; IAEA country profiles; EU statements.

nodes.label: Tumo and PicsArt
nodes.full: The Tumo Center for Creative Technologies, an after-school centre for teenagers founded by the diaspora philanthropists Sam and Sylva Simonian and opened in Yerevan in 2011, has taught animation, game design and programming to tens of thousands of students and has been copied in other countries; the photo-editing application PicsArt, founded in Yerevan in 2011 by Hovhannes Avoyan, became in 2021 one of the first companies founded in Armenia to be valued above one billion dollars.
nodes.src: Tumo Center and PicsArt company reports; Armenian and international press.

nodes.label: Areni-1
nodes.full: The excavations of Areni-1 by the Armenian archaeologist Boris Gasparyan and a joint international team reported in 2010 a leather shoe of about 3500 BC, the oldest known, and in 2011 a wine-making installation of about 4100 BC, both preserved by the cave's dry conditions; the finds became a national symbol of the antiquity of Armenian viticulture.
nodes.src: Pinhasi et al., PLoS ONE (2010); Barnard et al., Journal of Archaeological Science (2011).

nodes.label: Minsk Group
nodes.full: The OSCE Minsk Group, co-chaired from 1997 by France, Russia and the United States, mediated for three decades the plans of a phased settlement (1997), the Key West talks of 2001, the Madrid Principles of 2007 and the Kazan document of 2011, which foresaw the return of districts to Azerbaijan, an interim status for Karabakh and a later vote on its status; none was signed. Paralysed after 2022 by the war in Ukraine, the group was formally closed on 1 September 2025 after a joint request of Armenia and Azerbaijan.
nodes.src: OSCE statements and Madrid Principles (2007); OSCE Ministerial Council decision (1 September 2025); de Waal 2003, 2010.

nodes.label: Russian alliance
nodes.full: Armenia joined the Collective Security Treaty in 1992, accepted a Russian military base at Gyumri under an agreement of 1995 later extended to 2044, relied on Russia as its security guarantor and in 2015 joined the Eurasian Economic Union; after the war of 2020 and the attacks of 2022 and 2023, in which Armenia felt the alliance had not worked, Pashinyan froze its participation in the CSTO in February 2024 and began to take back control of border posts, among them the airport at Yerevan. Armenia has not left the union or the organisation, and still depends on Russia for energy and trade.
nodes.src: Treaties and agreements (1992, 1995, 2010, 2014); statements of Pashinyan (2023–2024).

nodes.label: European turn
nodes.full: The Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement with the European Union, signed on 24 November 2017 after the customs-union decision, entered into force on 1 March 2021; the EU's civilian monitoring mission in Armenia has watched the border since February 2023, and on 26 March 2025 parliament adopted a law declaring the start of the accession process, which Pashinyan has said would be decided by a referendum. Armenia has also said it will not leave the Eurasian union.
nodes.src: CEPA text (2017); EU Council decisions (2023); National Assembly records (26 March 2025).

nodes.label: Turkey and the closed border
nodes.full: Turkey closed the land border in April 1993 in support of Azerbaijan and after the occupation of Kelbajar; the Zurich Protocols of 10 October 2009 on diplomatic relations and the opening of the border were never ratified. The special envoys, named in 2021, agreed on air freight, and after the Turkish earthquake of February 2023 aid trucks crossed at Margara for the first time in decades; in 2025 the two sides agreed to reopen the Gyumri–Kars railway and to ease the passing of third-country nationals, and as of mid-2026 the border remains officially closed and Turkey links the full opening to a peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan.
nodes.src: Zurich Protocols (2009); Armenian and Turkish foreign ministries' statements (2021–2026); Armenpress reports.

nodes.label: Iran
nodes.full: Iran, with which Armenia has a short border at Meghri, became a trading outlet and a partner in an exchange of Iranian gas for Armenian electricity after the pipeline of 2007, in a North–South road corridor project towards Georgia and the Black Sea, and a political counterweight; Tehran has treated Armenia's Syunik border as a matter of its own security, which shaped its reaction to the plans for a transit route in 2025.
nodes.src: Iran–Armenia agreements; Armenian and Iranian press and official statements.

nodes.label: Diaspora and dual citizenship
nodes.full: The diaspora of several millions, far larger than the population of about 3 million, built relations with the republic through the All-Armenian Hayastan Fund of 1992, the Lincy Foundation of Kirk Kerkorian, the Birthright Armenia programme of 2003 and the permission of dual citizenship in 2007; the relations were marked by hopes and also by the diaspora's disagreements with the governments over the Karabakh compromise.
nodes.src: Law on Citizenship (2007); Hayastan Fund and Birthright Armenia reports.

nodes.label: Washington declaration
nodes.full: At a meeting in the White House on 8 August 2025, Pashinyan and Aliyev with President Trump signed a joint declaration, the foreign ministers initialled the text of a peace treaty and a route through Armenia's Syunik linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, named the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, was foreseen under Armenian sovereignty and with American participation; the treaty is not signed or ratified as of October 2026, and its supporters see an end to the war while critics in Armenia see a concession.
nodes.src: Joint declaration of Washington (8 August 2025); Armenian and Azerbaijani foreign ministries' statements.

nodes.label: Lake Sevan
nodes.full: Lake Sevan, whose level had been lowered by about 20 metres since the 1930s for irrigation and power, was the subject of a restoration programme under which the Arpa–Sevan tunnel and a limit on the water taken helped the level to rise by several metres after 2000, while the algal blooms of the warm summers, the fishing and the building on the shore remained problems.
nodes.src: Ministry of Environment reports; Lake Sevan Basin studies (2005–2020).

nodes.label: Emigration and census
nodes.full: The population of Armenia, which was about 3.3 million at the census of 1989 and was estimated at some 3.5–3.7 million in the early 1990s, fell by an emigration of several hundred thousand in the years of the blockade and to about 2.96 million in the census of 2022, with a low birth rate and an imbalance between the sexes at birth, one of the highest in the world in the 2000s.
nodes.src: Armenian Statistical Committee censuses (1989, 2001, 2011, 2022); UNFPA reports.

nodes.label: Refugees
nodes.full: Some 300,000 Armenians left Azerbaijan from 1988 to 1992, and some 200,000 Azerbaijanis left Armenia, a number that sources give variously; in 1992–1994 Armenia also received displaced persons from Karabakh, and in September–October 2023 about 100,000 from Karabakh came in a few days, equivalent to about three per cent of the population of the country.
nodes.src: UNHCR and Armenian migration service figures; de Waal 2003.

nodes.label: Covid-19
nodes.full: The first case of Covid-19 was recorded on 1 March 2020 and a state of emergency was declared on 16 March; the health system, overloaded in the autumn waves and in the weeks of the war, reported more than 8,000 deaths by 2022 among some 420,000 recorded cases, and excess-mortality estimates are higher.
nodes.src: Armenian Ministry of Health; WHO and Our World in Data compilations.

nodes.label: Women and domestic violence law
nodes.full: Women held about a quarter of the seats in the parliament elected in 2018 and about a third of those elected in 2021, after the party-list quotas were raised in several stages, and the law on the prevention of domestic violence, adopted in December 2017 after years of campaigning by women's organisations, came into force in 2018; the women's organisations also took part in the marches of the 2018 revolution and in the support work for refugees after 2020.
nodes.src: Electoral Code of Armenia; Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence (2017); Council of Europe and UN Women reports.

nodes.label: Karabakh Armenians in Armenia
nodes.full: The roughly 100,000 who left Karabakh in 2023, many of them women, children and elderly people, were housed in hotels, schools and rented flats, and the government set up a housing and cash-support programme; after two years many were still living in unstable conditions, and a share moved on to Russia and to Europe. The community's leaders have called for a right of return under international guarantees, which Azerbaijan says is open to them only as citizens of Azerbaijan.
nodes.src: UNHCR and Armenian government reports (2023–2025); statements of Karabakh Armenian organisations and of Azerbaijan.

nodes.label: Missing and prisoners
nodes.full: The families of the several thousand missing of the war of 1991–1994, of those of 2020 and of the soldiers and civilians detained in Baku after the war, have continued their search under the work of the International Committee of the Red Cross and of national commissions; the return of prisoners was a recurring subject in the peace talks, and as of 2026 some twenty Armenians, among them the former leaders of Karabakh sentenced in Baku in February 2026, remain in custody there, a matter on which the two governments describe the cases differently, Azerbaijan as trials of war crimes and Armenia as political.
nodes.src: ICRC reports; Armenian and Azerbaijani commissions' statements; reports on the Baku trials (2025–2026).

nodes.label: Minorities
nodes.full: Armenia is more than ninety per cent Armenian by population; the Yazidi Kurds, the largest of the minorities and numbering several tens of thousands, the Russians, the Assyrians and the Molokans keep their own schools, press and temples, and the Yazidi temple at Aknalich in Armavir, consecrated in 2019, is said to be among the largest in the world; the number of Yazidis has been falling because of emigration.
nodes.src: Armenian censuses (2011, 2022); Council of Europe Framework Convention reports.

nodes.label: Migrant workers
nodes.full: Hundreds of thousands of Armenians, in the construction trades and in services, worked seasonally or permanently in Russia, and their remittances, which were some ten per cent or more of the gross domestic product in some years, supported households in the provinces; in 2022 the movement went in the other direction, as tens of thousands of Russians, many in technology and the media, and their families moved to Yerevan.
nodes.src: Central Bank of Armenia remittance data; World Bank reports; Armenian press.

nodes.label: The Karabakh movement and independence
nodes.full: The Karabakh movement of 1988, the Sumgait pogrom, the Spitak earthquake and the independence acts of 1990–1991 set the conditions in which the Armenian republic came into being and the war began.
nodes.src: background — see the Soviet Caucasus 1953–1991 folio (caucasus-1953-1991)

nodes.label: The killings and deportations of 1915
nodes.full: The mass killings and deportations of the Ottoman Armenians in 1915, which Armenia and the diaspora call a genocide, remain the central reference of the republic’s memory and foreign policy.
nodes.src: background — see the Anatolia 1908–1923 folio (anatolia-1908-1923)
